claims.text: The baseline high-entropy alloy is uniformly mixed and superconducting under standard cryogenic testing.
The concentration of one chosen element can be varied while preserving the alloy's high-entropy phase.
Changes in target-element concentration alter the alloy's electronic structure.
Changes in target-element concentration alter the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Elemental distribution in the alloy directly affects the density of states at the Fermi level.
The density of states at the Fermi level affects electron-phonon coupling strength.
Electron-phonon coupling strength governs the superconducting transition temperature.
Changing the target-element concentration should produce a measurable variation in superconducting transition temperature.
Increasing the concentration of the chosen element should increase the density of states at the Fermi level.
A higher density of states at the Fermi level should produce a higher superconducting transition temperature relative to the baseline.
A lower density of states at the Fermi level should produce a lower superconducting transition temperature relative to the baseline.
The baseline alloy has a known superconducting transition temperature under standard conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains single-phase and avoids significant phase separation or additional microstructural changes.
Phase separation or additional microstructural changes could independently affect superconductivity.
Local structural disorder and variations in interatomic distances could confound the proposed concentration-to-transition-temperature relationship.
